why.support: Influencers get paid to make you want things. Their words, pictures and music are all chosen on purpose. Spot who's paying, and you decide what you want.
why.core: Influencers are paid to make you want things, and the best ones make it feel like advice from a friend. Every choice in their videos is deliberate: the words, the lighting, the music, the order of the shots. When you can spot who's paying and how the techniques work, you decide what you want, not them.
why.extend: Influencer content blends personal voice with commercial purpose. Its persuasive power comes from multimodal choices (language, image, sound and structure) that build trust and desire. Analysing those choices, and the commercial relationship behind them, lets you read the post as the advertisement it often is.

articles.title: Is it a review, or an ad?

body.support:
**Influencers** earn money when followers buy things. Even if you're under 16, you still see their videos.

**How they get paid**

- A brand pays them to post: **sponsored**.
- A brand gives them free stuff.
- They earn money from their **discount code**.

**Paid posts must be clear.** Look for **#ad** or **Paid partnership**.

**The tricks.**

- **Words:** *obsessed*, *honestly*, *you NEED this*. Feelings, not facts.
- **Pictures:** **close-ups**, bright light, before and after.
- **Sound:** happy, upbeat music.
- **Ending:** *Link in bio! Selling out fast!*
- **Friendship:** *Hey besties!* They talk like your friend.

**Unbox any post.** Who's paying? What tricks? What's missing? Then you decide.
body.core:
**Influencers** make money by getting their followers to like, try and buy things. Even if you're under 16 and can't have an account on platforms like TikTok or Instagram, you still see their videos: on YouTube without logging in, in group chats, and in ads.

**How influencers get paid**

- A brand pays them to post: a **sponsored** post.
- A brand sends free products, called **gifted** items.
- They earn money each time you buy through their **discount code** or **affiliate link**.

**The law says paid posts must be clear.** In Australia, it's against the law to mislead people. If an influencer is paid or gifted something, they need to **disclose** it clearly, with labels like **#ad** or **Paid partnership**, where you'll see them. Vague tags like *#sp*, *#collab* or *#ambassador*, hidden among twenty other hashtags, may not be clear enough.

**The techniques.** Every part of an influencer video is chosen on purpose.

- **Words.** *Obsessed*, *honestly*, *life-changing*, *you NEED this*. These are **subjective**: feelings, not facts.
- **Pictures.** **Close-ups** feel personal, like a friend talking to you. Bright light and perfect rooms make everything look better. **Before and after** shots tell a story.
- **Sound.** Upbeat music and trending sounds make you feel good and keep you watching.
- **Structure.** A hook in the first three seconds. A problem. The product fixes it. Then a call to action: *link in bio, selling out fast!*
- **Relationship.** *Hey besties!* They talk like your friend, so you trust them like one.

**Unbox any post.** Ask: Who's paying? What techniques are used? What's left out, like the price, the side effects, or the reviews that weren't so good? Then decide for yourself.
body.extend:
**Influencers** earn money from attention. Their income depends on persuading followers to buy things. Under-16s can no longer hold accounts on platforms like TikTok and Instagram. But they still see influencer content through YouTube (without logging in), shared links and ads.

**How influencers are paid:** **sponsored** posts, **gifted** products, and commission from **discount codes** and **affiliate links**.

**Disclosure.** Australian law bans misleading conduct. If an influencer is paid or gifted something, the post should **disclose** it clearly, where people will see it (for example, **#ad** or a **Paid partnership** label). Vague tags like *#sp*, *#collab* or *#ambassador*, buried in hashtags, may not be clear enough.

**The techniques work together.**

- **Language:** **subjective** words (*obsessed*, *life-changing*) and words like *literally* and *honestly* make opinion sound like proof.
- **Image:** **close-ups** feel personal. Lighting and styling make the setting look perfect. Before-and-after shots tell a problem-and-solution story.
- **Sound:** music and trending audio set the mood and keep you watching.
- **Structure:** a hook, a problem, the product as the answer, then a call to action, often with pressure (*selling out fast*).
- **Relationship:** talking like a friend (*hey besties*) builds trust.

**Analyse any post.** Who benefits? Which techniques are used? What's left out: the price, the risks, the bad experiences?

caseStudies.title: The influencer check-up

body.support:
The **ACCC** protects shoppers. In **2023**, it checked **118 influencers**.

What it found:

- **81%** had posts that were a problem.
- In **fashion**, it was **96%**.

The biggest problem? Not saying that a brand had **paid** them.

Some used words like *spon* or *collab*. Lots of people don't know what those mean.

So always check: who's paying?
body.core:
The **ACCC** is the government agency that protects shoppers. In **2023**, it checked the posts of **118 influencers** on Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat, YouTube, Facebook and Twitch. Members of the public had tipped the ACCC off about them.

It released what it found in **December 2023**:

- **81%** of the influencers had made posts that **raised concerns** under consumer law.
- In **fashion**, it was **96%**.
- In **gaming and tech**, it was **73%**.

The most common problem? Influencers **not disclosing** that a brand had paid them or given them something.

The ACCC also flagged **vague labels**: *sp*, *spon*, *sponcon*, *collab*, *ambassador*. Many people don't know what they mean, so they may not make it clear the post is an ad.

The ACCC said it would keep watching, and could take action against influencers and businesses that keep breaking the rules.
body.extend:
The **ACCC** is Australia's consumer watchdog. After tip-offs from the public, it reviewed the posts of **118 influencers** on Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat, YouTube, Facebook and Twitch. It reported what it found in **December 2023**.

- **81%** of the influencers had made posts that raised concerns under consumer law.
- The rate was highest in **fashion** (**96%**). It was lower, but still high, in **gaming and tech** (**73%**).

The most common problem was **not disclosing** brand deals. The ACCC also flagged **vague labels** (*sp*, *spon*, *sponcon*, *collab*, *ambassador*). Many people may not realise these mean a post is an ad.

The ACCC said it would keep watching, and could take action against people who kept breaking the rules.

The findings show that the selling purpose of a post is often hidden. So it's up to viewers to read carefully.

model.text:
**The post:** A fitness creator's reel about “GlowFuel” protein powder.

**Who is paying?** The caption ends with #ad. The discount code is her own name, so she earns money from each sale.

**Techniques.** She uses before and after photos. She says “I honestly can't live without it”. A timer says the code ends tonight. That makes people rush.

**What is left out?** The price: $79 a tub. There is also no proof that the powder caused the change.

**My view:** It is an ad that is made to feel like advice from a friend.

teacher.overview: Students analyse influencer content as persuasive multimodal texts. They learn how influencers are paid (sponsorship, gifting, discount codes, affiliate links), what clear disclosure looks like, and how language (subjective, evaluative words), images (close-ups, lighting, before-and-after), sound and structure (hook, problem, solution, call to action) work together to position viewers. The case study is the ACCC's December 2023 review of 118 influencers. The final task analyses a real post and writes what it's really selling.
prep: Choose 3–4 real influencer posts or videos students can view without an account (e.g. logged-out YouTube, or screenshots). Avoid gambling, alcohol, vaping and adult content.
Check your school's rules on showing social media content in class, especially for under-16s.
Projector and speakers: the sound technique matters.

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** sponsored posts, gifted products, discount codes and affiliate links. Paid posts must be disclosed clearly, e.g. #ad or Paid partnership. Techniques: subjective words (obsessed); close-ups, lighting, before-and-after; upbeat music.

**Video:** 1 hook (close-up and command); 2 problem (dim before shot); 3 reveal (slow motion, light, music); 4 after (filter, subjective word); 5 hidden disclosure (claims not sponsored, but #collab buried); 6 call to action (code, link, scarcity).

**Sort:** #ad at the start — clear ad; #sp in hashtags — hidden ad; cousin's shoes — not an ad; Paid partnership label — clear ad; not sponsored but a code — hidden ad; gift with #collab — hidden ad.

**Techniques (samples):** bright lighting — everything looks perfect, so the product seems to make life better; upbeat music — happy, energetic, want to keep watching; before and after — a story where the product is the hero; obsessed — sounds like honest proof, but it's a feeling; selling out fast — pressure to buy now.

**Case study:** 81% had posts raising concerns; 96% in fashion; non-disclosure was most common; vague labels may not be understood as ads; fashion relies heavily on gifted products and lifestyle content.

realityCheck: **Most students under 16 no longer hold accounts on the major platforms,** but they still see influencer content. Use logged-out viewing, screenshots or teacher-chosen examples.
**Some students want to be influencers.** Use it: understanding the techniques is the first step to using them honestly (see Make Content That Counts).
**Pick examples carefully.** Avoid gambling, alcohol, vaping, diet and adult content.
**Don't shame students for buying things.** The goal is informed choices, not guilt.
**Works in a real class:** yes. It's highly engaging, and pairs with The Odds Are Against You and Buy Smart Online.
